dct_description_sm: Several shear zones known in the crystalline basement of Alberta were active during the Paleoproterozoic assembly of Laurentia. Two continental-scale shear zones are traced from the Canadian Shield beneath the sedimentary cover of the Western Canada Sedimentary Basin: The Great Slave Lake shear zone (GSLSZ) in the northwestern corner of the province and the Snowbird tectonic zone (STZ) across central Alberta. On the Canadian Shield two major northerly trending shear zones mapped in Northwest Territories straddle the border into northeastern Alberta, where their traces bend to southeast and are covered by Devonian strata of the Western Canada Sedimentary Basin. Initially named Warren and Allan shear zones (Godfrey, 1958; Langenberg, 1983; Godfrey, 1986a), they were renamed Leland Lakes shear zone (LLSZ) and Charles Lake shear zone (CLSZ), respectively (e.g., McDonough et al., 2000). Each of them consists of a braided system of anastomosing subvertical 0.5 to 3-km wide splays of ductile mylonites. Names of these splays have been introduced by Pană et al. (2007): two sub-parallel, curvilinear, 50 to 500-metre wide belts of subvertical mylonites were separated as the Leland Lakes shear zone (the northwestern splay) and the Bocquene River shear zone (the southeastern splay). The Charles Lake shear zone consists of a braided system of anastomosing subvertical 0.5 to 3-km wide splays of ductile mylonites. From west to east, these splays are the Goldschmidt Lake, Mercredi Lake, Charles Lake and Bayonet Lake shear zones. A third major shear zone called the Andrew Lake shear zone proposed by McDonough et al. (2000) could not be confirmed by subsequent mapping. The crosscutting relationships between shear zones and adjacent granitoids are very complex, indicating concurrent deformation and granitoid intrusion during the ca. 2.0–1.9 Ga Taltson tectonothermal event (e.g., McDonough et al., 2000c). The Black Bay and Grease River shear zones mapped in Saskatchewan project below Lake Athabasca, in Alberta.
